title: Italian cuisine
wiki_lead:
Italian cuisine is a Mediterranean cuisine consisting of the ingredients, recipes and cooking techniques developed in Italy since Roman times, and later spread around the world together with waves of Italian diaspora. Significant changes occurred with the colonization of the Americas and the consequent introduction of potatoes, tomatoes, capsicums, and maize, as well as sugar beet—the latter introduced in quantity in the 18th century. Italian cuisine is one of the best-known and most widely appreciated worldwide. In 2025, Italian cuisine was listed as intangible cultural heritage by UNESCO.
The cuisine includes deeply rooted countrywide traditions as well as diverse regional dishes. Many dishes that were once regional have proliferated with variations throughout the country. Italian cuisine is one of the most popular and copied around the world. Italian cuisine has left a significant influence on several other cuisines around the world, particularly in East Africa, such as Italian Eritrean cuisine, and in the United States in the form of Italian-American cuisine.
A key characteristic of Italian cuisine is its simplicity, with many dishes made up of few ingredients, and therefore Italian cooks often rely on the quality of the ingredients, rather than the complexity of preparation. Italian cuisine generated an estimated €251 billion in global foodservice revenue in 2024, according to Deloitte. Over the centuries, many popular dishes and recipes have often been created by ordinary people more so than by chefs, which is why many Italian recipes are suitable for home and daily cooking, respecting regional specificities, privileging only raw materials and ingredients from the region of origin of the dish and preserving its seasonality.
The Mediterranean diet forms the basis of Italian cuisine, rich in pasta, fish, fruits, and vegetables. Cheese, cold cuts, and wine are central to Italian cuisine, and, along with pizza and coffee (especially espresso), form part of Italian gastronomic culture. Desserts have a long tradition of merging local flavours such as citrus fruits, pistachio, and almonds with sweet cheeses such as mascarpone and ricotta or exotic tastes as cocoa, vanilla, and cinnamon. Gelato, tiramisu, and cassata are among the most famous examples of Italian desserts, cakes, and patisserie. Italian cuisine relies heavily on traditional products; the country has a large number of traditional specialities protected under EU law. Italy is the world's largest producer of wine, as well as the country with the widest variety of indigenous grapevine varieties in the world.

History

Italian cuisine has developed over the centuries. Although the country known as Italy did not unite until the 19th century, the cuisine can claim traceable roots as far back as the 4th century BC. The foundation of Italian cuisine dates back to ancient Rome, where elaborate preparations can be found documented in a cookbook (Apicius).
However, the fall of the Roman Empire significantly changed Italian cooking, when different cities began to separate and form their own traditions based on climate, local agriculture and trade connections. Through the centuries, neighbouring regions, conquerors, high-profile chefs, political upheaval, and the discovery of the New World have influenced its development. Many different types of bread and pasta were made, and there was a variation in cooking techniques and preparation.
Trade, the location on the Silk Road, and its routes to Asia also influenced the local development of special dishes. Due to the climatic conditions and the different proximity to the sea, different basic foods and spices were available from region to region. Regional cuisine is represented by some of the major cities in Italy. grok_lead: Italian cuisine encompasses a diverse array of regional cooking traditions originating from Italy, emphasizing the use of fresh, high-quality local ingredients, simple preparation techniques, and a balance of flavors that reflect the country's varied geography and history. It forms a core component of the Mediterranean diet, a cultural practice shared across several countries including Italy, which was inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2010 for its knowledge, rituals, and traditions related to crops, fishing, animal husbandry, and communal meals. In December 2025, "Italian cooking, between sustainability and biocultural diversity" was inscribed on UNESCO's Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity, recognizing its role in fostering social bonds, sustainability, and artisanal food production. This recognition complements the cuisine's alignment with Mediterranean diet principles, as Italian restaurants commonly offer numerous healthy options such as vegetable-forward dishes, seafood, and light sauces. The roots of Italian cuisine trace back to ancient Roman times, with the first known cookbook, De Re Coquinaria attributed to Marcus Gavius Apicius in the 1st century AD, featuring recipes that incorporated spices, fish sauces, and elaborate presentations. Following the fall of the Roman Empire in 476 CE, medieval influences led to greater regional homogeneity in cooking, but the 15th and 16th centuries marked a transformation with the introduction of New World ingredients like tomatoes, potatoes, and corn via explorers such as Christopher Columbus, which gradually integrated into dishes despite initial resistance. By the 19th century, unification efforts and publications like Pellegrino Artusi's 1891 La scienza in cucina e l'arte di mangiar bene âthe first modern Italian cookbookâhelped standardize and promote a national culinary identity while preserving local variations, which had sold over 200,000 copies by the time of Artusi's death in 1911. Key characteristics of Italian cuisine include its regional diversity, driven by Italy's diverse climates and terrains: northern regions like Lombardy favor butter, rice, and meats in dishes such as risotto alla Milanese; central areas like Tuscany highlight olive oil, beans, and simple pastas like pappardelle; while southern locales including Campania emphasize tomatoes, seafood, and spicy elements in staples like pizza Margherita, created in 1881 to honor Queen Margherita of Savoy. Essential ingredients across regions encompass extra-virgin olive oil, pasta, cheeses like Parmigiano-Reggiano (produced since the Middle Ages under strict regulations), fresh herbs such as basil and oregano, and wines integral to both cooking and dining. Meals typically follow a structure of antipasti (appetizers), primi (pasta or rice), secondi (main proteins), contorni (sides), and dolci (desserts), promoting moderation and seasonality as per Mediterranean principles. Globally, Italian cuisine has profoundly influenced international food culture, with signature dishes such as pizza (particularly Margherita), widely regarded as the most iconic and popular Italian dish worldwide, pasta preparations like spaghetti carbonara, lasagna, and fettuccine Alfredo, and desserts including tiramisu and gelato achieving widespread popularity. This influence is particularly evident in the United States, where immigrant waves from the late 19th century onward introduced adapted versions like spaghetti and meatballs, leading to approximately 45,000 Italian restaurants as of 2025. Its emphasis on authenticity and quality has spurred movements for protected designations, such as the EU's Protected Designation of Origin for products like prosciutto di Parma, ensuring traditional methods and reinforcing Italy's culinary export dominance, with pasta and wine seeing significant growth in global markets.
